Content:
Just as the derivative of a function represents the slope of the tangent line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well.

Content:
To illustrate, consider the surface [MATH: z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2] and the plane [MATH: x=3.] The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point [MATH: P(3,2,5)] is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d4f24d622a4e949b317785d90718b43f]

Content:
To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}] and evaluate it at [MATH: P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (∂f)/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(18 − x^{2} − y^{2}); = − 2y; (∂f)/(∂y)|_{P}|= − 2(2); = − 4]

Content:
Note: To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line.

Content:
To find the equation of the downward parabolic curve, we can substitute the equation of the plane ([MATH: x=3]) into the equation of the surface ([MATH: f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2]). Doing this, we get

Content:
[MATH: f(3, y)|= 18 − 3^{2} − y^{2}; = 9 − y^{2}.]

Content:
So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is [MATH: z=g(y) = 9-y^2.] In the [MATH: yz]-plane, this curve has the following graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/81e19db2b630e94b015c3e8ad731743e]

Content:
To find the slope of the tangent to [MATH: g(y)] at [MATH: P,] we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate [MATH: g(y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: P(3,2,5).] This gives

Content:
[MATH: g^{′}(y)|= − 2y; g^{′}(2)|= − 2(2); = − 4.✓]

The curve [MATH: C] is the intersection of the surface [MATH: z = f(x,y)] with the plane [MATH: y=\pi.] So, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point [MATH: P(1,\pi,-1)] will be given by the partial derivative [MATH: \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,\pi)}.]

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative [MATH: \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}] at [MATH: (1,\pi)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: (∂z)/(∂x)|_{(1, π)}|= π\cos (1 ⋅ π) + \cos π; = π(− 1) + (− 1); = − π − 1]

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

[MATH: z − z|_{(1, π)}|= (∂z)/(∂x)|_{(1, π)}(x − 1); z − (− 1)|= (− π − 1)(x − 1); z + 1|= (− π − 1)x + π + 1; z|= − (π + 1)x + π]

The equation above represents a line in the [MATH: xz]-plane. The [MATH: xz]-plane through the point [MATH: P(1,\pi,-1)] has the equation [MATH: y=\pi.]

So, the tangent line to the curve [MATH: C] at [MATH: P(1,\pi,-1)] is given by the intersection of the following planes: [MATH: {y = π; z = − (π + 1)x + π]

sections.normalized_html: The curve [MATH: C] is the intersection of a surface [MATH: S,] defined by [MATH: z=f(x,y),] with the plane [MATH: y=1.] Given that the point [MATH: P(0,1,1)] lies on [MATH: C,] and that [MATH: f_x = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},] find a tangent vector to [MATH: C] at [MATH: P.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The curve [MATH: C] is the intersection of the surface with the plane [MATH: y=1.] So, the slope of the tangent to the curve [MATH: C] at the point [MATH: P] will be given by the partial derivative [MATH: f_x(0,1).]

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative [MATH: f_x(x,y)] at [MATH: (0,1)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f_{x}(0, 1)|= (sqrt(2)π)/(4)\sin (2(0) + (π(1))/(4)); = (sqrt(2)π)/(4)\sin ((π)/(4)); = (π)/(4)]

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

[MATH: z − f(0, 1)|= f_{x}(0, 1)(x − 0); z − 1|= (π)/(4)x; z|= (π)/(4)x + 1]

The equation above represents a line in the [MATH: xz]-plane. The [MATH: xz]-plane through the point [MATH: P(0,1,1)] has the equation [MATH: y=1.]

So, the tangent line to the curve [MATH: C] at [MATH: P(0,1,1)] is given by the intersection of the following planes: [MATH: {y = 1; z = (π)/(4)x + 1]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Just as the derivative of a function represents the slope of the tangent line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well.

Content:
To illustrate, consider the surface [MATH: z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2] and the plane [MATH: x=3.] The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point [MATH: P(3,2,5)] is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d4f24d622a4e949b317785d90718b43f]

Content:
To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}] and evaluate it at [MATH: P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (∂f)/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(18 − x^{2} − y^{2}); = − 2y; (∂f)/(∂y)|_{P}|= − 2(2); = − 4]

Content:
Note: To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line.

Content:
To find the equation of the downward parabolic curve, we can substitute the equation of the plane ([MATH: x=3]) into the equation of the surface ([MATH: f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2]). Doing this, we get

Content:
[MATH: f(3, y)|= 18 − 3^{2} − y^{2}; = 9 − y^{2}.]

Content:
So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is [MATH: z=g(y) = 9-y^2.] In the [MATH: yz]-plane, this curve has the following graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/81e19db2b630e94b015c3e8ad731743e]

Content:
To find the slope of the tangent to [MATH: g(y)] at [MATH: P,] we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate [MATH: g(y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: P(3,2,5).] This gives

Content:
[MATH: g^{′}(y)|= − 2y; g^{′}(2)|= − 2(2); = − 4.✓]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Geometric Interpretation of the Partial Derivative

Content:
To recap, when we calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},] we differentiate [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: y] and treat [MATH: x] as a constant. This is the same as finding the intersection of [MATH: z = f(x,y)] with the plane [MATH: x = x_0] and calculating the slope of the resulting curve.

Content:
So, we have the following result:

Content:
> Suppose that a surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and a plane [MATH: x = x_0] intersect on a curve [MATH: C,] and suppose that [MATH: P(x_0,y_0,z_0)] lies on [MATH: C.] Then [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}] evaluated at [MATH: P] gives the slope of the tangent to [MATH: C] at [MATH: P.]

Content:
We have a similar result for the intersection of a surface and a plane [MATH: y=y_0\mathbin{:}]

Content:
> Suppose that a surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and a plane [MATH: y = y_0] intersect on a curve [MATH: C,] and suppose that [MATH: P(x_0,y_0,z_0)] lies on [MATH: C.] Then [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}] evaluated at [MATH: P] gives the slope of the tangent to [MATH: C] at [MATH: P.]
